questions.stem: In a three-period moving average, the answer is written against:
options: a new period at the end
questions.why: The average of three consecutive figures is centred on the middle one. Writing it against the first period is the most common error.
whyNot: That would misalign the whole trend.
Also misaligned.
The average belongs to an existing period, not a new one.

questions.stem: Sales are Jan 42, Feb 50, Mar 46. What is the three-month moving average for February?
questions.why: (42 + 50 + 46) / 3 = 138 / 3 = 46.0, written against February as the middle month.
whyNot: That is February's raw figure, not the average.
That is January's raw figure.
That is the total before dividing by three.

questions.stem: Why is there no moving average for the first and last periods of a series?
options: There is no data on one side to include in the average
The data for those periods is always unreliable
Averages cannot be calculated for the ends
questions.why: A three-period average needs a figure before and after. Inventing one for the ends loses marks.
whyNot: The data is fine; the window simply does not fit.
They can be, if you have the surrounding data.
Seasonality is unrelated to where the series starts.

questions.stem: Why does a four-quarter moving average need centring?
options: Four is an even number, so the average falls between two quarters
questions.why: With an even number of periods, the midpoint of the window sits between two quarters. Averaging two consecutive four-quarter averages puts the figure back on a quarter.
whyNot: The issue is arithmetic, not data quality.
Size is not the problem.
Averaging removes seasonal variation; centring fixes the alignment.

questions.stem: Two consecutive four-quarter averages are 100.0 and 105.0. What is the centred average?
questions.why: (100.0 + 105.0) / 2 = 102.5, written against the quarter between them.
whyNot: That is the total before dividing by two.
That is the first of the two averages.
That is the difference between them.

options: Extending a past trend beyond the available data to estimate future values
Plotting two variables against each other
questions.why: Extrapolation projects the line forward. Its weakness is the assumption that conditions continue, which is what tends to fail.
whyNot: That is a moving average.
That is a scatter graph.
That is seasonal adjustment.

questions.stem: Why is 'correlation is not causation' an important point in a forecasting answer?
options: Two variables moving together does not prove one causes the other, so the forecast may rest on a false link
Causation is impossible to establish in business
questions.why: Both variables may be driven by a third factor, or the relationship may be coincidence. Building a forecast on a coincidental relationship produces a confident and worthless number.
whyNot: It can be measured and shown on a scatter graph.
It is harder to establish, not impossible.
Showing correlation is exactly what they do.

questions.stem: What is a specific weakness of moving averages as a forecasting tool?
options: They lag, so a genuine turning point shows up late
They cannot be calculated from quarterly data
questions.why: Smoothing is the point and the problem: by averaging across periods, the technique responds slowly, so a real change in direction is not visible until several periods after it began.
whyNot: Quarterly data is one of the standard applications.
They smooth fluctuations rather than exaggerating them.
They are calculated from a time series, not a scatter graph.
